extracted.intended_audience: Members of Congress, congressional staff, DOD and agency officials, and oversight bodies involved in A-76 competitive sourcing
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and conducting public–private competitions under OMB Circular A-76 (competitive sourcing), including required procedures, cost-comparison rules, organizational constructs (PWS, MEO), oversight mechanisms, and policy options—with specific attention to military medical facilities. The guidance covers definitions, process requirements, timelines, appeals/oversight, and congressional options to change implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of inherently governmental activity
rubrics_metrics.description: An inherently governmental activity is an activity that is so intimately related to the public interest as to mandate performance by government personnel. These activities require the exercise of substantial discretion in applying government authority and/or in making decisions for the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inherently governmental activities normally fall into two categories: the exercise of sovereign government authority or the establishment of procedures/processes related to oversight of monetary transactions or entitlements. The Circular lists four illustrative characteristics: (1) binding the United States to take or not take action by contract, policy, regulation, authorization, order, or otherwise; (2) determining, protecting, and advancing economic, political, territorial, property, or other interests by military or diplomatic action, civil or criminal judicial proceedings, contract management, or otherwise; (3) significantly affecting the life, liberty, or property of private persons; and (4) exerting ultimate control over acquisition, use, or disposition of U.S. property or establishing policies/procedures for collection/control/disbursement of appropriated funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual inventories of commercial and inherently governmental activities (FAIR Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal agencies must prepare and submit annually inventories of their commercial activities performed by federal employees to OMB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These inventories identify which activities are considered commercial (subject to competition) and which are inherently governmental (not subject to competition). The FAIR Act inventory requirement is a prerequisite for applying A-76 reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance Work Statement (PWS) completeness and role
rubrics_metrics.description: A Performance Work Statement (PWS) must describe the work to be performed and serve as the basis for the competition; agencies must ensure both the government’s bid (MEO) and private sector contractor proposals reflect all functions and personnel called for in the PWS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PWS should include all responsibilities and requirements, performance standards, acceptable deviations from the standards, and how the contract will be monitored. The Independent Review Official (IRO) analyzes the PWS for clarity and completeness; the IRO analysis provides the baseline for all cost estimates and is critical to valid cost comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Most Efficient Organization (MEO) development and firewall requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The MEO is developed by a team of federal employees (and sometimes a private sector contractor) and represents the government’s in-house bid (a streamlined reorganization of personnel). A 'firewall' must prohibit communication between members of the MEO and members serving on the PWS team.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MEO teams are typically composed of managers and bargaining-unit employees familiar with the tasks. The firewall is intended to insure fairness in the competition. The MEO exists only if it wins the competition; when the MEO wins, a letter of obligation implements the decision; when a contractor wins, a contract is awarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum cost differential requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: No activities may be converted between government in-house performance and contractor performance unless there is a minimum cost differential of $10 million or 10%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This minimum is established to prevent conversions based on 'marginal estimated savings'—the MEO must show savings of at least $10M or 10% relative to the private sector contractor’s costs to win.

rubrics_metrics.name: PMA scorecard and competitive sourcing goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Competitive sourcing was a Presidential Management Agenda (PMA) initiative; agency progress is evaluated with a red-yellow-green scorecard used to chart progress on PMA initiatives and set agency study goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PMA scorecard exerts pressure on agencies to meet targets (example: Army goals to study tens of thousands of positions by FY2009). The existence of PMA targets may influence agency prioritization and resource allocation for A-76 studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadlines and appointment of competitive sourcing officials (2003 Circular)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2003 revision established new deadlines for completion of A-76 studies (12 months for standard competitions and 90 days for streamlined competitions) and required appointment of competitive sourcing officials (e.g., Human Resource Advisor, Agency Tender Official, PWS Team Leader, Source Selection Authority, Contracting Officer, Competitive Sourcing Official).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These structural timelines and official roles are intended to standardize and speed competitions; DOD-specific legal/timeframe limits (e.g., a 30-month limit cited for certain DOD actions) should be noted when applying deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility/authority to use pre-2003 rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies (e.g., DOD) may seek permission to apply pre-2003 Circular rules to competitions initiated before the revised Circular; OMB may grant extensions or authority to use prior procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using pre-2003 vs revised procedures can materially affect timelines, procedures, and outcomes; agency requests and OMB approvals are part of oversight and can alter how a competition is governed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent review and oversight mechanisms (IRO, AAA, GAO protests, appeals)
rubrics_metrics.description: A-76 competitions are subject to oversight mechanisms: the IRO analyzes the PWS; the Army Audit Agency (AAA) can review and certify MEO bid proposals; protesters can file challenges with GAO; parties may appeal certifying decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oversight bodies can reverse or withdraw certifications (examples: AAA withdrew its certification and later reversed decisions). The presence and effectiveness of these mechanisms influence confidence in the integrity of cost comparisons and awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of external factors (BRAC, wartime casualty load, resource constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: External events—such as Base Realignment and Closure (BRAC) decisions, wartime casualty surges, mobilization, resource constraints, and facility condition—must be considered when deciding whether to conduct or implement A-76 competitions at specific sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report cites how BRAC inclusion put WRAMC in 'limbo', impeded capital investments, and contributed to recruitment/retention problems; similarly, high casualty loads and war mobilization may justify regulatory relief or suspension of A-76 at treatment facilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Option to exempt DOD from A-76 during declared war or mobilization
rubrics_metrics.description: The revised Circular states the Department of Defense Competitive Sourcing Official (without delegation) shall determine if the circular applies to DOD during times of declared war or military mobilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercising this opt-out could avoid personnel shortages and operational disruption at military medical facilities during high operational tempos; the report recommends providing Service Secretaries opportunity to apply for regulatory relief from A-76 in wartime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely completion of competitions to avoid destabilization
rubrics_metrics.description: Competitions must be completed within reasonable/established timeframes; protracted competitions (years long) can destabilize workforces, cause attrition of skilled personnel, hiring freezes, and operational gaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The WRAMC example shows that a competition spanning six-plus years contributed to staff shortages and service deterioration; adherence to the Circular’s deadlines (and enforcement) is a corrective measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure both MEO and contractor proposals reflect all functions and personnel
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must ensure that both the government’s MEO bid and private contractor proposals fully reflect all functions, tasks, and personnel required by the PWS for accurate cost comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incomplete or inconsistent inclusion of functions/costs can lead to invalid cost comparisons and reversals; oversight (IRO, AAA reviews) should validate completeness and comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit inclusion of health care and retirement costs in cost-comparison process for military medical facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: One option is to prohibit the inclusion of health care and retirement costs from the A-76 cost comparison process when evaluating military medical facility activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excluding certain categories (health care, retirement) could materially change the comparative economics and may be recommended to prevent inappropriate conversion of medical functions that carry embedded personnel/benefit costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine certain activities at military medical facilities to be inherently governmental
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could determine that all activities at military medical facilities are inherently governmental and therefore not subject to A-76 competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a policy option that would remove medical facility functions from competitive sourcing entirely, based on arguments about mission-criticality, patient safety, and public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit establishment of numerical quotas for A-76 studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could prohibit agencies from establishing numerical quotas (e.g., target numbers of positions) for A-76 studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing quota incentives would reduce pressure to pursue competitions for marginal savings and mitigate perverse incentives to meet PMA targets at the expense of operational considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require specific reporting on status of ongoing A-76 competitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies could be required to provide regular, detailed reports to Congress on the status of ongoing A-76 competitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandatory reporting increases transparency and oversight, helping Congress identify prolonged competitions, implementation problems, or workforce impacts early (e.g., to intervene or legislate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish rotating acquisition professionals as Agency Tender Officials (ATOs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could require establishment of a team of acquisition professionals to rotate services as Agency Tender Officials to oversee competitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using experienced acquisition professionals as ATOs would professionalize tendering, reduce mistakes, and provide continuity/competence in executing competitions and resolving complex acquisition issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require enforcement of A-76 rules and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must enforce A-76 procedural rules and ensure accountability throughout the competition to prevent mismanagement and adverse outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes following Circular deadlines, maintaining firewalls, proper certification of cost estimates, and ensuring responsible leadership—report cites failures of leadership and the system at WRAMC as causes of problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant federal employees rights comparable to private contractors in dispute processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative options include granting federal employees the same or comparable rights as private sector contractors—for example, access to expedited bid-protests or representation in appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing symmetric rights could level procedural imbalances and improve fairness in protests and appeals arising from A-76 competitions (H.R. 1585 provisions referenced include expedited bid-protests by federal employees).

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage and consider alternatives to A-76
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could encourage alternatives to A-76 for achieving efficiencies, such as different sourcing models, shared services, or management reforms that do not require public–private competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report suggests considering other approaches where A-76 is not appropriate (e.g., military medical settings) to avoid detrimental operational consequences of outsourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancel outstanding A-76 studies conducted under the pre-2003 Circular
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid problems associated with protracted or outdated procedures, Congress could direct cancellation of outstanding competitions initiated under the pre-2003 Circular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report notes stakeholders (e.g., AFGE) called for cancellation of long-running studies (example: Keesler AFB) that violated OMB timelines and undermined process integrity.
